    MultiSolid-CL

    MultiSolid-CL simulates gas flow, heat transfer, as well as gas-gas and gas-solid reactions in packed-bed reactors. It provides a Python simulation engine, a command-line interface for YAML-defined cases and batches, and a desktop application for projects, parameter studies, plots, and Excel reports. Simulations use DAETools, with an optional compiled SUNDIALS backend. Run data are saved as NetCDF with a JSON provenance manifest.

    Install the desktop application

    The first public desktop release is pending. Once published, download it from GitHub Releases (online). Until then, use the source installation below, or follow Build MultiSolid from a checkout to create a Linux or Windows distribution. After the documented system prerequisites, run python3.12 tools/build_desktop.py --headless on Ubuntu 24.04, or py -3.11 tools/build_desktop.py in Windows PowerShell. Each creates an isolated build environment and a validated portable archive.

    The Windows distribution targets Windows 11 x64. Choose one release asset:

    Asset Installation
    MultiSolid-<version>-windows-x64-setup.exe Run the installer, then open MultiSolid from the Start menu. Installation is for the current user.
    MultiSolid-<version>-windows-x64-portable.zip Extract the entire ZIP into a new folder, then run MultiSolid/MultiSolid.exe. Keep its files and subfolders together.

    Both distributions include Python, DAETools, Graphviz, and the compiler and libraries needed for Compiled execution. End users do not need to install these separately. GitHub's automatically generated source archives are source code; choose the installer or portable ZIP for the ready-to-run application.

    Create projects in a writable folder outside the application directory. The first Compiled run may take several minutes to build its model; compatible later runs reuse the project's cache. To update a portable installation, extract the new version into a new folder and open your existing project. The GUI guide explains the project workflow.

    Install the full repository from source

    Use Python 3.11 or 3.12 and Git. These steps install the engine, CLI, desktop application, compiled-backend Python dependencies, and DAETools plotter support in one environment. Windows and Linux need a matching DAETools distribution and its native dependencies.

    1. Get the source and create an environment

    These instructions use the application-and-ui branch, which contains the engine and desktop layout described here.

    git clone --branch application-and-ui https://github.com/Griminir5/multisolid-CL.git
cd multisolid-CL
python -m venv .venv

    Activate the environment in PowerShell:

    .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

    Or in a Linux shell:

    source .venv/bin/activate

    Use python3.11 or python3.12 to create the environment if your default python is a different version. Run the remaining repository commands from its root.

    2. Install the Python packages

    python -m pip install -e ".[compiled,plotter]" -e ./desktop

    Editable installation makes local Python changes available without reinstalling. The desktop package includes Excel export dependencies. Release builds use a separate, pinned environment described in the Windows build guide.

    3. Install DAETools

    Download DAETools 2.6.0 (online) for your operating system and Python version. Extract it, then, with the same virtual environment active, install from the extracted DAETools directory:

    python -m pip install .

    Follow the DAETools installation instructions for its native dependencies. The distribution must include the solver adapters you intend to use; the supplied single-case example uses SuperLU. Compiled execution also uses DAETools to build the model and solve its initial conditions. Return to the MultiSolid repository root after installation.

    4. Install the external tools

    • Linux desktop libraries: install the GUI prerequisites listed in the Linux build instructions, including libxcb-cursor0 on Ubuntu. Python's Qt wheel still needs these native libraries for X11 startup.
    • Graphviz: install the native Graphviz distribution with neato on PATH, or set MULTISOLID_GRAPHVIZ to the full path of its executable. This supplies the chemistry graph and CLI system diagram; no Python Graphviz binding is needed.
    • C++ compiler: for source Compiled execution, install GCC or Clang on Linux and make it available on PATH; CXX can select its executable. On Windows, install Visual Studio Build Tools with C++ x64 support; the application locates its toolchain through the Visual Studio installer.

    Without a managed native bundle, Compiled execution uses the pinned scikit-sundae==1.1.3 wheel's SUNDIALS runtime. Arbitrary system SUNDIALS libraries are not interchangeable with that runtime. Compiled KLU requires the managed bundle. See native bundles for staging the Windows compiler, solver libraries, and Graphviz runtime. Source execution also detects staged bundles under desktop/vendor/.

    5. Check the installation and launch

    python -m packed_bed examples/simulations/default_case/run.yaml --validate-only
packed-bed-ui

    python -m packed_bed_ui also launches the desktop application. To run the supplied case from the terminal:

    python -m packed_bed examples/simulations/default_case/run.yaml

    Validation of built-in definitions does not need DAETools. Python plugins may load their own dependencies during validation; see the CLI validation notes. Execution requires the selected solver and its dependencies. Each case run can replace files in its output directories; use separate directories to retain earlier results.

    Repository structure

    Path Purpose
    packed_bed/ (online) Simulation engine, CLI, configuration, scientific definitions, and reports
    packed_bed/compiled/ (online) Native code generation, compiler integration, and SUNDIALS runtime support
    desktop/ (online) Desktop package metadata, Windows build instructions, and installer definition
    desktop/packed_bed_ui/ (online) PyQt6 application, project storage, editors, studies, and Excel export
    docs/ (online) Model equations and the plugin, GUI, and CLI guides
    examples/simulations/ (online) Complete single-case and batch YAML inputs
    examples/plugins/ (online) Illustrative plugin packages
    plugins/ (online) Additional scientific plugins
    tools/ (online) Runtime staging, wheel builds, desktop freezing, and release checks
    .github/workflows/ (online) Native runtime CI

    Generated runtimes, build outputs, and caches are excluded from Git. Licences and scientific provenance notes stay beside the components they describe.

    Development

    Use the editable source installation above. Keep release builds separate from the development environment; the Windows build guide defines the pinned release inputs and acceptance checks.

    Useful starting points are configuration and validation (online), model equations (online), initialization (online), operating programs (online), simulation execution (online), and reports (online). Desktop navigation starts in window.py (online); project persistence is in project.py (online).

    Use scientific plugins for new species, property correlations, or reaction families that can be distributed independently. Changes to built-in definitions should retain their scientific references, units, and concentration bases. Keep DAETools imports lazy where possible so input validation remains usable without the solver. When changing the model, preserve equation names, ordering, and solver incidence unless the change deliberately requires otherwise.

    Check the example inputs after configuration changes:

    python -m packed_bed examples/simulations/default_case/run.yaml --validate-only
python -m packed_bed batch examples/simulations/default_batch_case/batch.yaml --validate-only

    For native runtime changes, run the smoke check with a working compiler and a managed runtime including KLU. It checks all three Compiled solvers; the scikit-SUNDAE wheel alone cannot pass its KLU check. Linux bundles must work without LD_LIBRARY_PATH; rebuild old bundles with the current staging tools:

    python -m packed_bed.compiled.smoke

    For packaging changes, build both application wheels with the configured build dependencies installed:

    python -m pip wheel --no-deps --no-build-isolation --wheel-dir build/wheels . ./desktop

    The desktop's offline help is generated from the guides and the short screen pages in docs/help/. Generated HTML is checked in so source installations and ordinary wheels can open help without documentation build dependencies. After editing documentation, the help template, or the application version, rebuild and check it:

    python -m pip install --require-hashes -r tools/help-requirements.txt
python tools/build_help.py
python tools/build_help.py --check

    The build validates internal page links and anchors and renders equations into MathML. Search and styling are local assets. Release wheel builds reject stale help; the frozen application collects the same files from the UI wheel.

    Use complete reactor runs, balance diagnostics, and grid/tolerance comparisons when changing numerical behaviour. Input validation and native smoke checks alone do not validate a scientific model. Update the relevant documentation with changes to interfaces, equations, or defaults.

    Attribution and citation

    A Zenodo DOI is planned for the first release. Until it is issued, cite the repository (online) and record the version, Git commit, and access date used for your work. For example, replace the fields in this provisional citation:

    MultiSolid-CL contributors. MultiSolid-CL [Computer software]. Version VERSION, commit COMMIT. https://github.com/Griminir5/multisolid-CL (online) (accessed DATE).

    Once the first release is archived, this section will provide its Zenodo citation and DOI. Cite the scientific sources for the kinetics and property data you use as well: see the built-in kinetics references and the documentation shipped with each plugin. Run manifests record source and configuration provenance to help identify the implementation behind results.
